column1: The project SDK recommended for new SQL database projects is {{c1::Microsoft.Build.Sql}}.
column2:
Microsoft.Build.Sql supplies the build for SDK-style SQL projects. It supports modern .NET tooling. The original format uses a different build setup, so its project file is not interchangeable with the SDK-style one.
Review source

column1: A SQL project's build produces a {{c1::.dacpac}} artifact containing the compiled database schema model.
column2:
A DACPAC is a database deployment package that contains the compiled schema. It gives the deployment tool the desired object definitions. A normal project build does not use it as a backup of table rows.
Review source

column1: SDK-style SQL projects include .sql files in the project folder tree through {{c1::default globbing}}.
column2:
Globbing means including files that match a pattern. SDK-style projects pick up matching SQL files under the project folder without listing each one. Exclude a deployment-only file if it is not a model definition.
Review source

column1: Install the command-line SQL project templates with {{c1::dotnet new install Microsoft.Build.Sql.Templates}}.
column2:
The install command registers the template package with the .NET CLI. It does not create a project. Once installation is complete, the sqlproj template becomes available to dotnet new.
Review source

column1: With the SQL templates installed, create MyDatabaseProject using {{c1::dotnet new sqlproj -n MyDatabaseProject}}.
column2:
The sqlproj template creates a project with the supplied name. Its project file identifies the SDK and target. Build the resulting project separately when you need a DACPAC.
Review source

column1: Build the SDK-style project MyDatabaseProject.sqlproj with {{c1::dotnet build MyDatabaseProject.sqlproj}}.
column2:
The build compiles the modeled schema and writes a DACPAC if it succeeds. It does not connect to a target to apply changes. Publishing uses that artifact in a separate step.
Review source

column1: A default Debug build places a SQL project's .dacpac in {{c1::bin\Debug}}.
column2:
bin\Debug is the default output folder for a Debug configuration. A Release build uses a different configuration folder unless the project overrides the output location.
Review source

column1: A SQL project's target platform is stored in the {{c1::DSP}} property.
column2:
DSP identifies the schema provider for the target engine. It affects which language features the build accepts. For example, the Sql170 provider targets SQL Server 2025.
Review source

column1: Install SqlPackage as a global .NET tool with {{c1::dotnet tool install --global microsoft.sqlpackage}}.
column2:
The global installation makes SqlPackage available as a .NET command-line tool. Install a supported .NET SDK first. Installing the tool does not grant access to any database.
Review source

column1: SqlPackage applies a .dacpac to a database with {{c1::/Action:Publish}}.
column2:
Publish compares the DACPAC model with the target and executes changes. SourceFile points to the package and TargetConnectionString identifies the destination. Use Script for a preview that does not apply changes.
Review source

column1: Enable SQL code analysis during a project build with {{c1::RunSqlCodeAnalysis}} set to True.
column2:
RunSqlCodeAnalysis turns on checks of the SQL source during the build. SqlCodeAnalysisRules selects rules and how to report them. A finding only stops the build when it is treated as an error.
Review source

column1: SQL project configuration, including its target platform, resides in the {{c1::.sqlproj}} file.
column2:
The project file describes the build, including the target platform. The separate SQL files describe objects such as tables and views. Changing the target provider changes what the build accepts.
